title: Dreams in prison (Genesis 40)
hookLine: Joseph interprets dreams and asks to be remembered, and is forgotten two years

cards: A covered shift. A reference letter. A friend talked through a terrible night.
And the friend says, I won't forget this. Then weeks go by, and nothing. In Pharaoh's prison, two new prisoners arrive: the king's chief butler, who served his cup, and his chief baker.
Both have offended Pharaoh. Joseph, who now looks after the prisoners, is assigned to them.
One morning he finds them both miserable, and asks the kind of question a jailer doesn't usually ask: why do you look so sad today?

teach.b: They've each had a dream, and no one to explain it. Joseph says, in the King James Bible: "Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you." He doesn't claim the gift as his own.
The butler dreams of a vine with three branches, grapes ripening, and himself pressing them into Pharaoh's cup.
Joseph says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you back your job. Then Joseph asks one thing: "But think on me when it shall be well with thee."

The Hebrew verb is remember: remember me, mention me to Pharaoh, get me out. I was stolen from my land, he says, and I've done nothing to deserve this pit. Here, for once, Joseph speaks about what was done to him.
The baker tells his dream: three baskets of bread on his head, birds eating from the top one. Joseph doesn't soften it: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, from off you.
On Pharaoh's birthday, it happens exactly so.
The butler gets his cup back. The baker is hanged.

teach.h: YET DID NOT THE CHIEF BUTLER REMEMBER JOSEPH.
teach.b: And the chapter's last line, flat as a closed door: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him." The next chapter begins two full years later.

Some Christian readers hear a far-off echo at the cross, where a man dying beside Jesus asks, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. That man is answered the same day. Joseph asked, and waited two years.

how: Some Christians read Joseph's long wait in prison as a picture of trusting God through delay, and the words "remember me" are part of Christian prayer through the thief's request in Luke 23:42.

games.q: you're Joseph. you've just given the butler good news: in three days he'll be free. you're still a prisoner for nothing you did. what do you do?
o: say nothing; it's not your place.
ask him to remember you to Pharaoh.
games.why: "think on me when it shall be well with thee." the butler goes free, and forgets him for two full years.

practice: Remember a time someone forgot you, a promise not kept, a thank-you that never came, and be honest about it, the way Joseph was when he said, I have done nothing to deserve this.
Then breathe out and set it down, and think of one person you may have forgotten, someone whose kindness you never followed up. If you pray, you can pray for them both.

wordCard.voice: Joseph. The prisoner who interpreted two dreams, asked to be remembered, and was then forgotten for two years.

orig.note: Hebrew: to remember. Joseph asks the butler to remember him; the chapter ends with the butler not remembering.

carryVoice: Your line: remember me. The butler forgot for two whole years. Day three hundred sixty-nine.
